pos: n. (the Saxon mining town where Luther was born in 1483 and died in 1546)
etymology: German Eisleben, perhaps from a personal name with leben, an inheritance or estate; the older form is Islebia.
biblical_def: Eisleben in the county of Mansfeld was a copper mining town, and Martin Luther was born in it on 10 November 1483, the son of a miner who had come there for work and moved the family to Mansfeld within a year. Luther came back to Eisleben in January 1546, at the end of his life and in poor health, to arbitrate a quarrel between the counts of Mansfeld over mining rights; he preached four times in St Andrew's church, settled the dispute, and died in the early hours of 18 February in a house in the town, having answered Justus Jonas that he was ready to die holding the doctrine he had taught. His body was carried to Wittenberg. Johannes Aurifaber and Jonas were with him. The dictionary records Eisleben for the symmetry, and for the thing Luther was doing when he died, which was settling a dispute about money between two Christian lords. Paul's account of his own end fits it: a fight fought, a course finished, the faith kept, and a crown laid up by a righteous judge.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a course as a race and the ground run over; to finish as to complete; a crown as a reward of victory; a judge as one who decides; and to keep as to hold and preserve.
webster_full: COURSE, n. A passing; a moving or motion forward; the ground or distance passed over; a race; career.
FINISH, v.t. To arrive at the end of, in a figurative sense; to complete; to perfect; to bring to an end.
CROWN, n. An ornament worn on the head by kings; a garland; reward; honorary distinction; the top of the head.
JUDGE, n. A civil officer invested with authority to hear and determine causes; one who decides any question.
KEEP, v.t. To hold; to retain in one's power or possession; to preserve; to observe or fulfil, as a promise.
corruption_summary: Saxon copper-mining town where Luther was born in 1483 and where, having come to arbitrate a mining dispute, he died on 18 February 1546.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the shape Paul gives to the end of a life spent in the ministry, which is a finished assignment rather than an achievement: “I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith” (2Ti 4:7). What follows is not earned by that record but given by a judge, “which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day” (2Ti 4:8).

The live temptation with a figure like Luther is hagiography, which would prefer him to die preaching a great sermon rather than arbitrating a quarrel over copper. Paul holds his own life cheap next to the errand: “neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy, and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus” (Act 20:24). And the object in either case is not the man's reputation: “Christ shall be magnified in my body, whether it be by life, or by death” (Phi 1:20). Luther died in the town he was born in, settling someone else's dispute.

pos: n. (the Saxon county and town where Luther was brought up, and whose copper mines his father worked)
etymology: German Mansfeld, probably the field of Manno, a personal name, with Feld, a field.
biblical_def: Mansfeld was a small county in the eastern Harz, rich in copper shale, and the town of Mansfeld is where Luther grew up from the age of one. His father Hans Luder leased smelting furnaces there, rose to be one of the town's assessors, and sent his son to the Latin school in the town and then on to Magdeburg, Eisenach and Erfurt, intending him for the law. The household was hard, devout and anxious about money, and Luther's later writing on vocation, on the godliness of ordinary callings and on the fourth commandment is marked by it. The counts of Mansfeld quarrelled over the mines for decades; Luther died arbitrating between them in 1546. The dictionary records Mansfeld for the family and the furnaces. The Reformation's recovery of vocation, that a smelter or a housewife serves God in the work itself and not merely in the prayers around it, came in part out of this household, and Scripture had always said so: whatever is done is to be done heartily as to the Lord, and bodily labour is not a lower service.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a calling as a vocation and occupation; a vocation as the employment in which one is engaged; to serve as to work for; heartily as sincerely; and godliness as piety and a religious life.
webster_full: CALLING, n. A divine summons or invitation; vocation; employment; occupation or profession; the usual occupation.
VOCATION, n. A calling by the will of God; summons; employment; calling; trade; occupation.
SERVE, v.t. To work for; to bestow the labor of body and mind in the employment of another; to obey and worship.
HEARTILY, adv. From the heart; with all the heart; with sincerity; really; cordially.
GODLINESS, n. Piety; belief in God, with reverence and obedience to his commands; a religious life.
corruption_summary: Harz copper county and town where Luther was brought up and where his father leased smelting furnaces; the counts' mining quarrel drew Luther back in 1546.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that an ordinary calling is itself a service rendered to Christ. Paul says so to the lowest-ranked people in his congregations: “And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men” (Col 3:23), and again, “With good will doing service, as to the Lord, and not to men” (Eph 6:7). A man leasing furnaces in Mansfeld was in that position.

The live temptation is the medieval scale of holiness, in which the monk outranks the miner, and the Reformation's answer was not to despise devotion but to put it in proportion. Paul does exactly that: “For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things” (1Ti 4:8), which reduces austerities without reducing piety. And the apostolic ambition for ordinary Christians is modest and concrete: “to do your own business, and to work with your own hands, as we commanded you” (1Th 4:11). The son of the house made that a doctrine.

pos: n. (the Thuringian town where the Protestant princes formed their league in 1531 and adopted Luther's articles in 1537)
etymology: German Schmalkalden, from the stream Schmalkalde, the narrow or shallow water.
biblical_def: Schmalkalden, a small iron-working town in the Thuringian forest, gave its name to two things. In February 1531 the Protestant princes and cities, chiefly Electoral Saxony and Hesse, formed the Schmalkaldic League there for mutual defence after the Diet of Augsburg had rejected their confession; it became the political body of German Protestantism for fifteen years. And in 1537 the League met at Schmalkalden to decide whether to attend a general council summoned by Paul III; Luther, who was too ill to take part in the discussions, had written for the occasion the Schmalkald Articles, a short, blunt statement of what could not be conceded, which was later received into the Lutheran confessional books. The League was crushed at Mühlberg in 1547. The dictionary records Schmalkalden for the articles rather than the army. A list of things that cannot be given up is a useful document, and Scripture provides the pattern: hold fast the form of sound words, and contend earnestly for a faith once delivered.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an article as a particular item of a confession; a form as a model and pattern; to hold fast as to keep firmly; a league as an alliance; and to contend as to strive earnestly.
webster_full: ARTICLE, n. A single clause or item in an account; a particular; a distinct part of a writing or discourse; a point of faith.
FORM, n. The shape or external appearance of a body; a model; a pattern; established practice; a formula.
HOLD, v.t. To stop; to confine; to restrain; to keep in any particular state; to retain; to keep fast.
LEAGUE, n. An alliance or confederacy between princes or states for their mutual aid or defense.
CONTEND, v.i. To strive; to struggle in opposition; to dispute earnestly; to strive in debate.
corruption_summary: Thuringian town where the Schmalkaldic League was formed in 1531 and where Luther's Schmalkald Articles were laid before it in 1537.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the faith has a shape which can be written down and must be held. Paul gives the instruction in those terms: “Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus” (2Ti 1:13). Jude makes the deposit fixed and the defence of it a duty, since it “was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3).

The live temptation at Schmalkalden was to let the league become the confession, so that the political alliance mattered more than the articles it defended; Mühlberg settled that in 1547 and the articles outlived the army. What an overseer must be able to do is stated without reference to any alliance: “Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught” (Tit 1:9). And the boundary is drawn so high that no authority can move it: “But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8).

pos: n. (the Saxon mining town where Thomas Müntzer preached in 1520 and where the Zwickau Prophets arose)
etymology: From a Slavic name, perhaps Zwikowe, with later German spelling; the town stands on the Mulde.
biblical_def: Zwickau in Saxony grew on silver and then coal, and its church of St Mary holds a carved altar by Michael Wolgemut. The Reformation reached it early and then went past it. Thomas Müntzer was appointed preacher at St Mary's in 1520 on Luther's recommendation, quarrelled with the other clergy within months, preached against them, and was expelled in 1521; around the same time a group of Zwickau weavers led by Nikolaus Storch began claiming direct revelations, dreams and visions superior to Scripture. Three of them, the Zwickau Prophets, went to Wittenberg at the end of 1521 and unsettled Melanchthon and Carlstadt until Luther returned from the Wartburg and dealt with them. Müntzer went on to the Peasants' War and was executed in 1525. The dictionary records Zwickau for the test the Prophets forced. The question was never whether God can speak but whether a dream outranks a text, and Scripture answers it by commanding that the spirits be tried, and by fencing the gospel against an angel from heaven.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a prophet as one who foretells and one who instructs in religion; a spirit as an immaterial being; to try as to prove by a test; a dream as the thought of a sleeping person; and sound as orthodox and uncorrupted.
webster_full: PROPHET, n. One that foretells future events; a predicter; a foreteller; one who instructs others in religion by divine inspiration.
SPIRIT, n. The intelligent, immaterial and immortal part of human beings; an apparition; temper; a being of a superior nature.
TRY, v.t. To examine; to make experiment on; to prove by a test; to put to the proof; to sift.
DREAM, n. The thought or series of thoughts of a person in sleep; an idle fancy; a vain imagination.
SOUND, a. Entire; unbroken; healthy; founded in truth; firm; valid; orthodox; free from error.
corruption_summary: Saxon mining town where Müntzer preached in 1520 and the Zwickau Prophets claimed revelations above Scripture before unsettling Wittenberg in 1521.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the duty of testing, which belongs to the congregation and not only to its ministers: “believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world” (1Jo 4:1). The standard by which they are tried is fixed and public, and Paul sets it above any claimed messenger: “But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8).

The live temptation at Zwickau was not enthusiasm as such but the ranking, a dream placed above a text, and once that ranking is granted there is nothing left to appeal to. Paul says what Scripture is and what it is sufficient for: “All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness” (2Ti 3:16). And the LORD had already said that his written word is not a weak instrument needing supplement: “Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?” (Jer 23:29).

pos: n. (the Thuringian town where Wenceslaus Link and then Gabriel Zwilling preached, and where Luther mediated in 1522)
etymology: German Altenburg, the old fortress, from alt, old, and Burg, a castle.
biblical_def: Altenburg in eastern Thuringia was an electoral Saxon town with a castle and a collegiate chapter. Its Reformation was contested from the start: the town council wanted Gabriel Zwilling, an Augustinian who had led the radical changes at Wittenberg while Luther was at the Wartburg, and the chapter and the elector resisted him; Luther came to Altenburg in 1522 and again afterwards, preached, and advised on the appointment, and Wenceslaus Link, his old Augustinian colleague from Erfurt, served there as preacher before going to Nuremberg. Spalatin, the elector's chaplain and the man who had sheltered Luther's correspondence for years, became superintendent at Altenburg in 1525, married, and spent the rest of his life organising visitations in the district. The dictionary records Altenburg for Spalatin's second career. A courtier who had been at the centre of great events went to a small town and spent twenty years inspecting parish schools, and Scripture commends that order of things: he that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a superintendent as one who has oversight; a visitation as the act of visiting for inspection; least as smallest; much as a great quantity; and to reap as to gather a harvest.
webster_full: SUPERINTENDENT, n. One who has the oversight and charge of something, with the power of direction; an overseer.
VISITATION, n. The act of visiting; a judicial visit or official inspection of a diocese, school or church.
LEAST, a. Smallest; little beyond others, either in size or degree; the lowest in any scale.
MUCH, a. Great in quantity or amount; abundant; a great quantity; a great deal.
REAP, v.t. To cut grain with a sickle; to gather a harvest; to obtain; to receive as a reward.
corruption_summary: Thuringian town whose contested Reformation Luther mediated in 1522, and where Spalatin became superintendent in 1525 and spent twenty years on visitations.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Christ's own scale, which treats the small charge as the diagnostic rather than the consolation prize: “He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much” (Luk 16:10). Paul reduces the requirement on any servant of the church to a single quality: “it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful” (1Co 4:2).

The live temptation for a man who has been near great events is to find ordinary work beneath him, and Spalatin had been the elector's chaplain and Luther's protector before he went to inspect village schools. Paul warns against the weariness that such a change invites: “let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not” (Gal 6:9). The commendation in the parable is not for scale but for having been trustworthy with little: “thou hast been faithful over a few things” (Mat 25:21).

pos: n. (the Saxon see and margraviate on the Elbe, whose bishopric was dissolved in 1581 and whose porcelain came later)
etymology: German Meißen, from the stream Misni, a Slavic name; the margraviate took the castle's name.
biblical_def: Meissen on the Elbe was founded as a German fortress in 929 against the Slavs, became a bishopric in 968 as part of the mission to the Wends, and gave its name to the margraviate out of which Electoral Saxony grew. Its cathedral stands on the rock beside the Albrechtsburg castle. The diocese was caught in the division of Saxony: the Ernestine lands went Lutheran in the 1520s, the Albertine lands under Duke George stayed Catholic until his death in 1539, and the bishops of Meissen lost their authority piece by piece until Bishop John IX resigned his temporal rights in 1581 and the see lapsed. The Albrechtsburg later housed the first European hard-paste porcelain works from 1710. The dictionary records Meissen for the mission that founded it. A bishopric was planted on a frontier to preach to the Wends, and six hundred years later it was wound up by a Protestant elector; the work of preaching to a people was begun by one order of the church and continued by another, which is the ordinary way the word has travelled, since the growth belongs to God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a mission as a sending with a commission; a frontier as the border of a country; to plant as to set for growth; increase as augmentation; and to water as to supply with water.
webster_full: MISSION, n. A sending; the act of sending; persons sent; commission; charge; duty on which one is sent.
FRONTIER, n. The marches; the border, confine or extreme part of a country, bordering on another country.
PLANT, v.t. To put in the ground and cover, as seed for growth; to set in the earth for propagation; to settle.
INCREASE, n. Augmentation; a growing larger; that which is added; produce; profit; progeny.
WATER, v.t. To overflow with water; to wet or supply with water; to irrigate; to supply with drink.
corruption_summary: Elbe fortress and bishopric founded in 968 for the mission to the Wends, whose see lapsed in 1581 as Saxony divided and reformed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the men who plant and the men who water are both servants and neither supplies the result. Paul names both and then removes the credit from both: “I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase” (1Co 3:6). Luke measures the progress of a mission in a single sentence that mentions no bishop: “And so were the churches established in the faith, and increased in number daily” (Act 16:5).

The live temptation when one church order replaces another is to read the change as a verdict on everything that went before. Meissen was planted by Latin bishops among the Wends and reformed out of existence by a Protestant elector, and the preaching in that country never stopped. Paul describes the gospel itself as the thing that spreads, “as it is in all the world; and bringeth forth fruit” (Col 1:6). The end is the worship of the nations and not the survival of a see: “All nations whom thou hast made shall come and worship before thee, O Lord” (Psa 86:9).

pos: n. (the Saale see where Nicholas von Amsdorf was installed as the first Protestant bishop in 1542)
etymology: German Naumburg, the new fortress, from neu, new, and Burg, a castle.
biblical_def: Naumburg on the Saale holds a cathedral famous for the twelve life-sized donor statues in its west choir, carved about 1250, among them the Margravine Uta. Its chapter was Catholic and its see fell vacant in 1541, whereupon the Elector John Frederick of Saxony, who claimed the advowson, had Nicholas von Amsdorf, Luther's old friend and a Wittenberg professor, installed as bishop in January 1542, with Luther himself preaching and performing the ordination; it was the first attempt to continue the episcopal office in a Protestant form in Germany. The chapter refused to recognise him, elected Julius Pflug instead, and after the Schmalkaldic War Amsdorf was expelled in 1547 and Pflug took the see. The dictionary records Naumburg for the experiment. Luther ordained a bishop without any bishop present, on the ground that the office is one with the presbyterate and that a church may set apart its own overseers; the New Testament uses the words interchangeably, and what it requires of the man is a list of qualities and not a pedigree.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a bishop as an overseer; an elder as one older and a church officer; to ordain as to set apart to an office; to appoint as to designate; and an office as a duty conferred by authority.
webster_full: BISHOP, n. An overseer; a spiritual superintendent or ruler; in the primitive church, an elder or overseer of a particular church.
ELDER, n. One who is older; an officer in the Jewish and Christian churches; a person who rules or teaches in a church.
ORDAIN, v.t. To set apart for an office; to appoint; to invest with ministerial functions or sacerdotal power.
APPOINT, v.t. To fix; to constitute; to allot; to designate; to assign; to ordain or establish.
OFFICE, n. A particular duty, charge or trust conferred by public authority and for a public purpose; employment.
corruption_summary: Saale see where Luther ordained Nicholas von Amsdorf as the first Protestant bishop in 1542, against a chapter that elected Julius Pflug instead.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the New Testament describes one office under two names and attaches no pedigree to it. What is required is competence with the deposit: “Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9), and the ambition for it is honourable, “If a man desire the office of a bishop, he desireth a good work” (1Ti 3:1).

The live temptation in the Naumburg experiment was the one it did not escape, a bishopric still inside a prince's gift, so that an elector appointed and a war unappointed. The apostolic account of how such men come to their charge names a different agent entirely: the flock is one “over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers” (Act 20:28). And Peter addresses the same men as elders doing a bishop's work, “Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof” (1Pe 5:2), which is the ground Luther stood on when he ordained without a bishop.

pos: n. (the Saale see founded in 968, where the two pagan Merseburg charms survive in a cathedral manuscript)
etymology: German Merseburg, probably the fortress of Mers or of the marsh, with Burg, a castle.
biblical_def: Merseburg on the Saale was made a bishopric in 968, suppressed in 981 and restored in 1004, one of the frontier sees founded for the mission to the Slavs. Its cathedral library holds a tenth-century manuscript into which a monk copied, on a blank leaf of a liturgical book, two short charms in Old High German, one for freeing a captive and one for healing a horse's leg, invoking Wodan, Frija and other heathen gods. They are the only surviving pagan Germanic incantations in that language, and they survive because a Christian scribe wrote them into a church book. Georg of Anhalt was made the Protestant bishop of Merseburg in 1545, ordained by Luther. The dictionary records Merseburg for the charms. A people may be baptised while its charms are still in use, and the monk who wrote them down was probably not an unbeliever but a man collecting what the country folk said. Scripture's remedy for that condition is not secrecy but exposure to a better word, since its word is the fire and the hammer, and it calls believers to keep themselves from idols.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a charm as words or things supposed to possess occult power; an enchantment as the use of magic arts; an idol as an image worshipped; to keep as to preserve; and a hammer as an instrument of force.
webster_full: CHARM, n. Words, characters or other things imagined to possess some occult or unintelligible power; a magic power or spell.
ENCHANTMENT, n. The act of producing certain wonderful effects by the invocation of demons; incantation; magic arts.
IDOL, n. An image, form or representation, consecrated as an object of worship; a person or thing greatly loved.
KEEP, v.t. To hold; to retain; to preserve; to guard; to protect; to restrain from departing.
HAMMER, n. An instrument for driving nails, beating metals, and the like; any instrument applied by blows.
corruption_summary: Saale frontier see founded in 968, whose cathedral manuscript preserves the only surviving pagan Germanic charms in Old High German.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that superstition in a baptised country is answered by the word rather than by suppression. The LORD describes his own word in terms that need no help: “Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?” (Jer 23:29). John closes an epistle to Christians with the shortest possible charge about the residue of the old religion: “Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (1Jo 5:21).

The live temptation at a frontier see was syncretism, a Christian name laid over a heathen practice, and the Merseburg charms are physical evidence of it in a church book. Isaiah's verdict is as applicable to a horse charm as to a carved image: “They that make a graven image are all of them vanity” (Isa 44:9). What actually displaced such things in Saxony, over centuries, was preaching, and Luke records the mechanism in a city full of magic books: “So mightily grew the word of God and prevailed” (Act 19:20).

pos: n. (the Upper Lusatian town of the Six Towns league, known for its great painted Lenten veils)
etymology: From a Slavic name, perhaps Sitawa, the place of rushes; German Zittau.
biblical_def: Zittau in Upper Lusatia, at the corner where Saxony, Bohemia and Silesia meet, was one of the Six Towns whose league defended the roads of Lusatia from 1346. It grew wealthy on cloth, turned Lutheran in the 1520s, and lost its privileges after the Bohemian rising. It keeps two Lenten veils, large painted cloths once hung to hide the chancel through Lent: the Great Zittau Veil of 1472, eight metres by six, with ninety painted scenes from creation to judgment, and a smaller veil of 1573 showing the instruments of the Passion. The great cloth was used as a tent and a tarpaulin in later centuries and survives by accident. The dictionary records Zittau for the veils, which are a picture of a doctrine they now illustrate against themselves. A cloth was hung to shut the people out of the chancel through Lent, and the gospel declares that the veil of the temple was torn in two from the top down, and that believers have boldness to enter by a new and living way.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a veil as a cover that conceals; a chancel as the part of a church about the altar; to rend as to tear apart; boldness as confidence and courage; and to enter as to go or come in.
webster_full: VEIL, n. A cover; a curtain; any thing that conceals from the view; a cover worn by women to conceal the face.
CHANCEL, n. That part of the choir of a church between the altar or communion table and the balustrade that incloses it.
REND, v.t. To separate any substance into parts with force or sudden violence; to tear asunder; to split.
BOLDNESS, n. Courage; bravery; intrepidity; freedom from timidity; liberty of speech; confidence of access.
ENTER, v.i. To go or come in; to pass within the exterior limit of anything; to be initiated into.
corruption_summary: Upper Lusatian cloth town of the Six Towns league, Lutheran from the 1520s, which keeps the great painted Lenten veil of 1472.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the event the gospels report at the moment of Christ's death, which decided what veils are now for: “And, behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom” (Mat 27:51). The writer to the Hebrews draws the conclusion for worshippers in plain terms: believers have “boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus” (Heb 10:19).

The live temptation that a Lenten veil expresses is the screening off of holy things from ordinary people, which the medieval chancel arrangement did physically for forty days a year. The way in is described as opened and alive: “By a new and living way, which he hath consecrated for us, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh” (Heb 10:20). And the invitation that follows assumes access rather than distance: “Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith” (Heb 10:22). Zittau's cloth is best read now as a picture of what was taken down.

pos: n. (the Franconian fortress where Luther waited out the Diet of Augsburg in 1530)
etymology: German Coburg, perhaps the fortress of the cow pasture or of a personal name, with Burg, a castle.
biblical_def: Coburg in Franconia, the southernmost point of Electoral Saxony, has above it the Veste Coburg, one of the largest fortresses in Germany. Luther was still an outlaw under the Edict of Worms and could not safely go to Augsburg for the Diet of 1530, so he was left at Coburg, the nearest Saxon ground, while Melanchthon presented the Confession. He stayed from April to October with Veit Dietrich as his companion, worked on the Psalms and the Prophets, wrote a stream of letters urging Melanchthon to stop being afraid, learned at Coburg of his father's death, and preached to the household. He wrote to Melanchthon that he was tired of their anxiety, which was unbelief rather than prudence. The dictionary records Coburg for those six months, which are a study in waiting while other men act. Scripture has words for it: be not afraid of their faces, for I am with thee to deliver thee; and they shall fight against thee, but they shall not prevail against thee.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines afraid as struck with fear; to deliver as to free and rescue; to prevail as to overcome; a face as the front of the head and presence; and anxiety as painful uneasiness of mind.
webster_full: AFRAID, a. Impressed with fear or apprehension; fearful; struck with fear; terrified.
DELIVER, v.t. To free; to release, as from restraint; to set at liberty; to rescue from danger or evil.
PREVAIL, v.i. To overcome; to gain the victory or superiority; to be in force; to have effect.
FACE, n. The front part of an animal's head; the surface of a thing; presence; appearance; look.
ANXIETY, n. Concern or solicitude respecting some event, future or uncertain, which disturbs the mind.
corruption_summary: Franconian fortress where Luther, still an outlaw, spent April to October 1530 while Melanchthon presented the Confession at Augsburg.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Luther kept writing down the road to Augsburg, that fear of men is answered by a promise of presence and not by a calculation of odds. God's word to a young prophet is the text for it: “Be not afraid of their faces: for I am with thee to deliver thee, saith the LORD” (Jer 1:8), followed by a forecast that concedes the attack and denies the outcome, “they shall fight against thee; but they shall not prevail against thee” (Jer 1:19).

The live temptation is to call anxiety prudence, which is precisely the charge Luther laid against Melanchthon in those letters. The Psalmist's confession names an object instead of a probability: “I will say of the LORD, He is my refuge and my fortress: my God; in him will I trust” (Psa 91:2). And Isaiah describes the by-product of doing right rather than of winning: “the work of righteousness shall be peace; and the effect of righteousness quietness and assurance for ever” (Isa 32:17). Luther spent six months in a castle he could not leave, translating the Prophets.
